fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the parts I find most compelling, because it closes the loop between AI-driven design and real experimental evidence.

The agents designed a set of nanobody candidates aimed at newer viral variants, and rather than stopping at the computational predictions, we took those designs into the wet lab and actually tested how they bound. What came back was a mix: some candidates showed improved binding to the newer variants while keeping activity against the original target, and others didn't pan out.

The interesting thing is what you do with that signal. Those experimental results feed back into the next round. The agents can look at which designs worked, update their reasoning about what structural features matter, and propose a refined batch. So instead of one static shot at the problem, you get this iterative cycle where real measurements steer the AI toward better candidates each time.

For me that's the whole point. The models are powerful at generating and ranking hypotheses, but biology is full of surprises you can't fully predict from sequence and structure alone. Letting experiments ground and correct the agents is what turns it from a clever demo into something that can genuinely accelerate discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says the candidates were tested in the wet lab and those results feed into the next round, guiding updated reasoning and refined designs.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that experimental validation closes the loop. You can propose a nanobody that looks promising computationally, but the experiment tells you whether it actually behaves the way you hoped. And when it doesn’t, that’s useful information for deciding what to change next.

So the Virtual Lab becomes a way to iterate: generate hypotheses, design candidates, test them, and use those results to guide the next round. The important question is whether that feedback helps you make better decisions over time. Can you identify which changes improve binding while preserving other properties you care about? Can you choose experiments that distinguish between competing explanations?

That connection to experiments is what makes this interesting scientifically. The computational predictions are hypotheses, and the experimental results give you a way to challenge and refine them.

r001.rationale: The response says experimental results reveal how candidates actually behave and provide information for deciding what to change in the next round, grounding subsequent nanobody modifications.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find really interesting is that experimental validation can become part of the discovery process, rather than just a final check. The Virtual Lab can propose nanobody candidates, but those proposals are still hypotheses. When you actually test them, you learn which ideas hold up and where the reasoning was incomplete.

And the failures can be especially informative. If a candidate doesn’t perform well, is that because it doesn’t bind strongly enough, because it’s unstable, or because it’s difficult to produce? Those are different problems, and they should lead to different changes in the next round of design.

So the exciting possibility is this iterative loop: the AI helps formulate hypotheses, experiments provide feedback, and that feedback guides the next set of candidates. The key question is whether incorporating those results actually makes subsequent designs better. That’s a much more meaningful test than whether the system can generate a convincing scientific discussion.

r001.rationale: The response says actual experiments provide feedback that guides the next set of nanobody candidates and that failures should lead to changes in the next design round.
